stance_basis: letter explicitly states no ORV uses are appropriate on public lands in Alaska and urges rewrite of the draft EIS
summary: Friends of the Earth's Arctic Representative submitted a detailed letter opposing the draft Environmental Impact Statement for EO11644, arguing that no ORV uses are appropriate on Alaskan public lands except strictly controlled subsistence uses. The letter criticizes the draft as vague, incomplete, and mediocre, raising concerns about the open/closed status of BLM lands, inadequate treatment of non-recreational ORV uses, flawed economic impact analysis, and inappropriate claims about ORV use strengthening family relationships. FOE urges a complete rewrite of the draft with special consideration for Alaska's unique arctic and sub-arctic conditions.
complaint_summary: Friends of the Earth's Arctic Representative argues that no ORV uses are appropriate on Alaskan public lands (except strictly controlled subsistence uses), criticizes the draft EIS as vague, incomplete, and mediocre on issues including open/closed BLM land status, non-recreational ORV controls, economic impact analysis, and family-relationship claims, and urges a complete rewrite.

I am the "Arctic Representative" for Friends of the Earth, a national conservation organization of over 27,000 members with a membership of nearly 200 Alaskans. Our state has very large areas of Public Domain lands under Federal ownership and management. It is my urgent duty to comment to you upon Interior's EOll644 concerning the use of Off Road Vehicles on public lands and the subsequent Draft Environmental Impact Statement which your department has prepared for the Executive Order.
My comments are made strictly with Alaskan conditions in mind, but with the knowledge that application of these comments is pertinent to other states in which federal ownership is present, including those states in which the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Bureau of Reclamation have lands under their ownership or control. We are of course very especially mindful of interior Alaska's sub-arctic and arctic conditions and also the potential for heavy use of the ORV by all sectors - private commercial, ren-commercial, government, military, recreational and non-recreational - in our state which has few roads and many isolated sites of interest to the ORV user.
FOE appreciates the intent of EOll644, especially since it has, in cooperation with other organizations, instituted its own study of ORV use with an intention of developing model legislation for ORV uses.
FOE in Alaska would like to start with the position that no ORV uses are appropriate on public lands anywhere for any reason in Alaska. We do realize that some uses are necessary however, such as the uses of Natives and some Non-Natives for subsistence activities such as the gathering of firewood, fishing and hunting. In this light we grant that certain uses for ORVs are necessary, but only if under strict control, especially within the fragile ecosystems in Alaska.

In closing, I cite an example of the inappropriateness of some of the content and statements of your draft. You comment several times that one benefit of ORV use is a potential strengthening of the family structure or of family relationships. In Fairbanks some families have nearly or actually reached inter and intra family blows over the . bitter disputes of snowmobile uses. In the interior Native village of Humbes on the Kojukuk River the snowmobile has typically replaced the dogshid. A fathur nearly lost an arm this past winter due to severe frostbite suffered during a long return on foot after his snowmachine typically broke down on a subsistence hunting trip. Nearly every snowmachine in every village breaks down before winter's end. Many accidents occure. Many Natives also use the snowmachine to travel elsewhere to obtain alcoholic beverages not available in any Native Village and return in various drunken conditions, often to begin a long seige of family fighting and inter-family disputes.
In Alaska and elsewhere - such as in Minnesota - many families are torn apart as some family member is maimed or killed in the extraordinary number of serious accidents which characterize the recreational use of the snowmachine. In my own case a newly constructed snowmachine race track near my home outside Fairbanks has created unrest and dissention among the families nearby whose previously Alaskan quietness has been shattered with the agonizing noise of the weekend races.
